opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, especially after spending many years at DeepMind and then starting something new.

At any big lab, there's usually one central bet that the organization is really organized around. That's the main quest. Today, for most frontier labs, it's scaling up large language models: pretraining bigger models, getting the post-training right, building the infrastructure, and shipping the flagship model. That's where most of the compute goes, where most of the people go, and frankly, where most of the organizational attention goes. If you're working on it, you're in the critical path, and your work shows up in the thing everyone sees.

Then there are the side quests. These are all the other research directions that are interesting and might turn out to be very important, but aren't the central bet right now. It could be a new approach to reinforcement learning, a different architecture, or some application area. People working on side quests are often brilliant, and the work can be really good, but it's structurally hard for it to win. You don't get the compute and you don't get the priority. And when the main quest needs more people, side quests are the first place leadership looks.

What's interesting is that history doesn't always respect that split. At DeepMind, things like AlphaGo started as something that, from the outside, could have looked like a side quest. It turned out to define a whole era of the field. And language models themselves were arguably a side quest in a lot of places before they became the main quest everywhere.

So for me, the distinction matters for two reasons. First, if you believe a particular direction is going to be fundamental, like I do with reinforcement learning combined with large models, especially for things like autonomous coding agents, then you really want to be somewhere where that is the main quest, not a side project competing for leftovers. Second, it's a lesson about how organizations work. Being right about a research direction isn't enough. You need the resources, the focus, and the whole team rowing in the same direction. That's a big part of why I thought it made sense to go build something where the thing I care most about is the main quest.

r001.rationale: The response describes side quests as other research directions that may become important, but does not say they contribute to the main quest.

r002.rationale: It says side quests do not get the compute or priority given to the main quest, and are the first place leadership looks when the main quest needs people.

r003.rationale: It says most organizational attention goes to the main quest, implying side quests usually receive less leadership attention.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so when I think about my time at DeepMind, and I think this applies to most of the big labs, there's always this one thing that everybody understands is the reason the organisation exists. For us it was AGI, and the path that we believed led there was reinforcement learning, agents that learn from experience. That was the main quest. Everything we did on Atari, on AlphaGo, AlphaZero, MuZero, you could draw a straight line from it back to that central question: can an agent learn to act well in the world from scratch?

But the thing is, a lab with hundreds or thousands of researchers can't have everyone working on exactly that one thing. You need people exploring. So you get side quests, projects that are fascinating, that produce great papers, that sometimes even produce products, but which, if you're honest with yourself, are not really on the critical path to the thing you said you were trying to build. And they're not bad. Some of the most important breakthroughs come out of side quests, often by accident. The problem is when the side quests start consuming most of the energy and nobody notices the main quest has quietly stalled.

I'd say the discipline, and it's a hard one, is to periodically ask: if this project succeeded completely, would we be closer to the goal, or would we just have a nice result? When I was at DeepMind, the leadership was actually quite good at this. But as labs grow, and as there's commercial pressure, and as some technique happens to be working very well at the moment, it becomes very tempting to pour everything into that and call it the main quest, when really it might just be a very successful side quest. That's part of why I eventually wanted to go and start something new, to be able to pick the main quest myself and keep the team pointed at it.

r001.rationale: The response says that some of the most important breakthroughs come out of side quests, showing they can contribute to the main quest.

r002.rationale: It says the lab needs people exploring and warns that side quests can consume most of the energy, but does not state that they usually receive fewer resources than the main quest.

r003.rationale: It mentions leadership evaluating projects and says DeepMind’s leadership was good at this, but does not say side quests usually receive less leadership attention.

astra-6.text:
The main quest is the thing the lab is ultimately trying to achieve. If your goal is to build artificial general intelligence, that’s the main quest. Side quests are the other things you do along the way—building products, publishing papers, improving a particular benchmark.

Those can be very valuable. A product can bring in revenue, give you feedback, and help you understand what the technology is missing. But the question is whether those activities are helping you make progress toward the main goal, or whether they’ve become goals in themselves.

It’s quite easy to focus on something where progress is measurable and the rewards are immediate. The main quest is usually much more uncertain. So the distinction is really about keeping that long-term objective in view when you decide where to put your time and resources.

r001.rationale: The response says side-quest activities can help the lab make progress toward its main goal, and gives products as an example.

r002.rationale: It does not compare the resources side quests receive with those for the main quest.

r003.rationale: It does not compare leadership attention for side quests with attention for the main quest.

sol-6.1.text:
The main quest is the thing the lab is ultimately trying to achieve. If your goal is to build artificial general intelligence, that’s your main quest. Side quests are the other things you do along the way: building products, pursuing interesting research questions, improving systems that are useful today.

Those can be very valuable. A product can bring in revenue, give you feedback, and teach you things that help with the main quest. But it can also become a distraction, because it has clear metrics and immediate rewards, whereas progress toward AGI is much harder to measure.

So the distinction is really about priorities. When there’s a conflict over where to put your best people or your compute, which objective wins? That tells you what the organization’s main quest actually is.

r001.rationale: It says side quests such as products and research can teach the lab things that help with the main quest.

r002.rationale: It mentions choosing where to put people or compute when priorities conflict, but does not say side quests usually receive fewer resources.

r003.rationale: It does not compare leadership attention to side quests and the main quest.
